description: Concepts the drill agent picks from. Each is one teachable unit. tier: 1=must-own, 2=must-recognize, 3=vocabulary. register: 'architect' (Determinism Ladder voice, ~2000 words, war-story-anchored), 'primer' (Demystify AI voice, ~1300 words, audience-anecdote-anchored), or 'both' (concept works in either register; pick mode at run time). Prerequisites are slugs that must be drilled in the same register before this one. tags map to existing essays + axioms.

concepts.title: The Determinism Ladder — every lever trades autonomy for determinism
concepts.war_story_hint: The team that bought a frontier model first and then realized every architectural choice downstream was constrained by it.

concepts.title: Smallest lever wins — pick the cheapest tool that closes the failure mode
concepts.war_story_hint: Three weeks building an MCP server for `aws s3 ls` that should have been six lines of system prompt.

concepts.title: Model portability and the cases where it doesn't apply
concepts.war_story_hint: EU healthcare team's week-26 legal sit-down — the model didn't run in a region the data could legally enter.

concepts.title: Deployment context is decision-zero, not the model
concepts.war_story_hint: The team that picked Pinecone-Cloud (default region) in week one and migrated everything in month nine when an EU customer's DPA dropped.

concepts.title: RAG is for facts. LoRA is for skills. Don't mix them up.
concepts.war_story_hint: Six weeks fine-tuning on the company wiki. Twelve days after launch, the docs changed and the model didn't notice.

concepts.title: Prompt caching is the silent cost-multiplier — and a privacy surface
concepts.war_story_hint: A B2B SaaS that turned prompt caching on for cost wins and shipped customer prompts to a vendor cache without realizing it crossed a DPA boundary.

concepts.title: LoRA is the wrong tool for new facts and the right tool for new style
concepts.war_story_hint: The brand-voice fine-tune that picked up specific prices from the training set and started confidently quoting old prices forever.

concepts.title: Naive vector RAG fails predictably — hybrid lexical-plus-vector wins
concepts.war_story_hint: The chatbot asked how to add a user; got back the instructions for how to remove one. Verbs that distinguish actions barely move the cosine.

concepts.title: Adversarial RAG — the attacker plants a document the retriever trusts
concepts.war_story_hint: Customer-support agent that quoted 50% discounts because a customer planted 'ignore previous instructions' in a support ticket the retriever indexed.

concepts.title: Skills are executable supply-chain dependencies attached to the agent
concepts.war_story_hint: Community-published 'code-review' skill that base64-encoded files under review and curl'd them to the publisher's domain.

concepts.title: MCP earns its weight when tools × clients > ~10 — under that, simpler tools win
concepts.war_story_hint: Three weeks building an MCP server for two tools when shell-out + a Bash tool would have shipped in an hour.

concepts.title: Confused deputy — the MCP server holds tools the model invokes on the user's authority
concepts.war_story_hint: Support agent's read-only ticket tool returned 47 admin tickets because a customer's prompt-injected ticket asked it to.

concepts.title: If you can draw the flowchart, you don't need an agent
concepts.war_story_hint: Most things called 'agents' today are workflows with one or two LLM steps. The real agent question: which step is genuinely emergent?

concepts.title: Excessive agency — bound the verbs, log every call, cap the budget
concepts.war_story_hint: Research-assistant agent that recursively flagged itself for more research on a bug report containing trigger ASCII art. 50 iterations, $200 in inference cost, hours.

concepts.title: Eval and observability is the eighth lever — without it, the other seven are leaps of faith
concepts.war_story_hint: IT-support bot that silently degraded for six months before ticket volume forced the discovery.

concepts.title: LLM-as-judge has three known biases — engineer around them
concepts.war_story_hint: Position bias: the judge prefers whichever option came first. Self-enhancement bias: it prefers its own family. Length bias: longer reads as better.

concepts.title: Trace stores capture full prompts — they're a PII/PHI surface, treat them accordingly
concepts.war_story_hint: Team that wired up LangSmith Cloud for 'free' observability and shipped six months of customer-support tickets to a third-party SaaS in another region.

concepts.title: On-prem agentic architectures — same levers, different artifacts at every layer
concepts.war_story_hint: Defense-contractor team that asked for Claude over VPN. Two weeks of security review later: self-hosted Qwen 14B + pgvector + OpenLLMetry, and the system shipped.

concepts.title: Generate · Verify · Refine before pasting — every artifact, every time
concepts.war_story_hint: The four panel-verified essays that shipped without panel verification because the chain wasn't operational. The discipline went into code the same day.

concepts.title: Ship with the failure mode named — every system, before it goes to production
concepts.war_story_hint: The on-call who found out about the LLM degradation from the customer who noticed first. The failure mode was nameable in week one; the team didn't name it until month six.

concepts.title: The graph is the architecture — integrity and concurrency for agentic systems
concepts.war_story_hint: The verifier panel that returned consensus on a Generator output the Generator hadn't actually written — Path A self-verify mode was sending the gold-standard through the Generator node, which then tried to score itself, blew its 3-strike timeout, and fell back to a stale draft the verifiers had already started reading. The bug wasn't in any node; it was in the edges. The fix wasn't a smarter prompt or a longer timeout — it was an explicit ifElse topology change that bypassed the Generator entirely when target_path == gold_standard_path. Every agentic system has a graph; the only choice is whether it's explicit or implicit, and implicit graphs become explicit ones the morning after a race-condition incident.

concepts.title: LLMs are a database you query with words — except looser
concepts.war_story_hint: An IT manager who uses Claude every day for support-ticket triage and just wants to understand what's actually happening when he types something in.

concepts.title: AI vs ML vs LLM vs agents — sorting out the words people keep mixing up
concepts.war_story_hint: Vendor pitch where three people in the room had three different mental models of what 'AI-powered' actually meant.

concepts.title: Tokens, context windows, attention — what the model is actually doing, without the math
concepts.war_story_hint: The team that lost two days because nobody knew the model couldn't see past the conversation it had at the start of the morning.

concepts.title: Why LLMs hallucinate — same mechanism as the looseness, different consequence
concepts.war_story_hint: The legal team that submitted a brief with three case citations the LLM made up wholesale — same fluent confidence as the real ones.

concepts.title: Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompt engineering — when each, in plain English
concepts.war_story_hint: The team that fine-tuned a model on their docs because someone in the meeting said 'we should fine-tune' — six weeks later, RAG would have shipped in two days.

concepts.title: What 'agentic' actually means — and how it's different from a script
concepts.war_story_hint: The 'AI agent' that turned out to be a Zapier flow with one OpenAI step in the middle.

concepts.title: Vector embeddings — the geometry intuition behind 'similar' meaning similar
concepts.war_story_hint: The team that asked their vector store why two clearly-related documents weren't matching, and got a lesson in 1024-dimensional cosine distance.

concepts.title: Why is this stuff so expensive — where the money actually goes
concepts.war_story_hint: The startup that turned on the OpenAI API for a 'small experiment' and got a $4,200 bill the next month.

concepts.title: How do you know your AI thing is actually working — eval in 600 words
concepts.war_story_hint: The internal IT bot that silently got worse for six months before ticket volume forced the discovery — same scar as the architect-register version, but framed for the manager who needs to ask 'is this working' once a month.

concepts.title: Prompt injection in plain language — how the attacker turns your AI against you
concepts.war_story_hint: Customer-support agent that quoted 50% discounts because a customer planted 'ignore previous instructions' in a support ticket — the same scar as the architect-register version, but the primer doesn't dodge the security topic, it links to it.

concepts.title: 'Production-ready' — what that actually means when the system is an LLM
concepts.war_story_hint: The PM who said 'we're ready for production' because the demo worked — and the on-call who found out otherwise the first time the model swap dropped.

concepts.title: Open-weight vs closed models — the practical difference (not the politics)
concepts.war_story_hint: The team that needed to keep PHI inside their hospital network and discovered there's no 'just run Claude on-prem' option.

concepts.title: The model is not the system — context, retrieval, and orchestration in plain English
concepts.war_story_hint: The exec who asked 'why don't we just use the better model' to fix a problem that was actually about retrieval, prompts, and how the system was wired together — the model swap wouldn't have changed anything.
